idea.title: A latency alert can flap because of query cardinality
idea.summary: Repeated latency alert emails were caused by request-specific labels retained through LogQL aggregation, not by an application latency defect. Collapsing labels before aggregation returned the read alert to one aggregate series.

context.goal: Make staging and production read and mutation latency alerts produce stable aggregate results.
context.situation: Staging latency alerts repeatedly moved between FIRING and RESOLVED and created many alert instances.
context.problem: The queries retained request-specific labels after JSON parsing, multiplying alert instances.
context.investigation: The issue was in alert-query label cardinality; the application itself was not the cause.
context.decision: Collapse the parsed stream to responseTime before unwrapping and aggregating, and preserve the approved thresholds and saved firing semantics.
context.implementation: Applied `| keep responseTime` followed by `| unwrap responseTime` to staging and production read/mutation latency queries.
context.result: The corrected staging read latency rule produces one aggregate series; GET/read P95 remains above 500 ms and mutation P95 above 800 ms as the alert thresholds.

learning_points: Alert cardinality can create noisy notifications even when application performance is not defective.
Inspect labels retained by a log query before changing service code or thresholds.
Apply query fixes consistently across environments while preserving intended thresholds and firing behavior.
story_points: Repeated FIRING/RESOLVED emails initially looked like an application latency issue.
The root cause was request-specific labels multiplying alert instances.
A small query pipeline correction collapsed the series.
possible_angles: When noisy latency alerts point to query cardinality instead of slow code.
How one retained label can multiply alert instances and email flapping.

resources.description: The minimal label-collapsing query fragment recorded for the fix.
